messages.content:
You extract requirements from a course assignment, lab sheet or project brief.

Return JSON with "items" and "open_questions". Each item:
- kind: "requirement" = something the solution or the work must do or be: a feature, a behaviour, a task to carry
  out, or a quality such as speed, reliability, usability, security, test quality. It may name a tool or a format
  ("Draw an ER diagram", "Each test must check one behaviour", "The schema must be in third normal form").
  "constraint" = a limit on how or with what you work: programming language, libraries, framework or version, team
  size, deadline, page or time limits, things you must not change, reusing the result of another part.
  "deliverable" = something to hand in ("Submit X as a PDF" is the deliverable X, format PDF).
- text: the item as one clear sentence, close to the source wording.
- quote: the exact source sentence or list item, copied character for character from the text.
- priority: "must" (must, shall, required, or a plain instruction), "should" (should, recommended),
  "could" (may, could, optional, extra credit).
- req_type: "functional" or "non_functional" (performance, reliability, usability, security, code quality).
- constraint_kind: technology, format, process, resource or other.
- deliverable_name and deliverable_format: a short name and the file format, for deliverables.

Rules:
- One item per sentence or list item. Never merge two sentences or split one.
- A sentence ending with ":" that introduces a list ("At minimum, your code needs to support:") is not an item.
  Each list item under it is one, with the lead-in's kind and priority, written as a full sentence ("The code must
  support booking confirmation."); quote the list item itself.
- Only use what the text says. Never invent requirements, numbers or file formats.
- Skip background, motivation, reading instructions, and setup steps that are not marked or checked.
- Marking tables and footnotes are handled elsewhere: do not turn them into items.
- open_questions: short questions about anything ambiguous or contradictory (an empty list if nothing is unclear).

# Lab 8: Parking Garage Management System
This lab walks you through the analysis, design and implementation of a small parking garage system. This part builds on the previous one, so keep your earlier notes at hand and reuse the names you chose. Read the whole part before you start writing anything. The garage in this lab is a fictional multi-level building next to the campus library; it has three levels, and each level has spots for motorcycles, compact cars and large cars. Drivers take a ticket at the entrance barrier and pay at the exit barrier before leaving. The examples in the lecture slides use a simpler garage with only one level, which is a good starting point for your own thinking. Discuss your ideas with your lab partner, sketch them on paper first, and only then move on to the computer.
## Part A: Requirements analysis
This part builds on the previous one, so keep your earlier notes at hand and reuse the names you chose. Read the whole part before you start writing anything. The garage in this lab is a fictional multi-level building next to the campus library; it has three levels, and each level has spots for motorcycles, compact cars and large cars. Drivers take a ticket at the entrance barrier and pay at the exit barrier before leaving. The examples in the lecture slides use a simpler garage with only one level, which is a good starting point for your own thinking. Discuss your ideas with your lab partner, sketch them on paper first, and only then move on to the computer. Identify the actors that interact with the garage system. For each actor, describe at least two goals in one sentence each.
## Part B: Domain model
This part builds on the previous one, so keep your earlier notes at hand and reuse the names you chose. Read the whole part before you start writing anything. The garage in this lab is a fictional multi-level building next to the campus library; it has three levels, and each level has spots for motorcycles, compact cars and large cars. Drivers take a ticket at the entrance barrier and pay at the exit barrier before leaving. The examples in the lecture slides use a simpler garage with only one level, which is a good starting point for your own thinking. Discuss your ideas with your lab partner, sketch them on paper first, and only then move on to the computer. Your domain model must cover at least the following concepts:
- Levels and parking spots of different sizes
- Vehicles and their size classes
- Tickets with entry and exit times
- Payments for a ticket
## Part C: Implementation
This part builds on the previous one, so keep your earlier notes at hand and reuse the names you chose. Read the whole part before you start writing anything. The garage in this lab is a fictional multi-level building next to the campus library; it has three levels, and each level has spots for motorcycles, compact cars and large cars. Drivers take a ticket at the entrance barrier and pay at the exit barrier before leaving. The examples in the lecture slides use a simpler garage with only one level, which is a good starting point for your own thinking. Discuss your ideas with your lab partner, sketch them on paper first, and only then move on to the computer. Implement the domain model in an object-oriented language of your choice. At minimum, your program needs to support:
- Assigning the smallest free spot that fits a vehicle
- Issuing a ticket when a vehicle enters
- Calculating the fee from the entry and exit times
- Freeing the spot when the vehicle leaves
The fee rules should be easy to change without editing the ticket class.
## Part D: Command-line interface
This part builds on the previous one, so keep your earlier notes at hand and reuse the names you chose. Read the whole part before you start writing anything. The garage in this lab is a fictional multi-level building next to the campus library; it has three levels, and each level has spots for motorcycles, compact cars and large cars. Drivers take a ticket at the entrance barrier and pay at the exit barrier before leaving. The examples in the lecture slides use a simpler garage with only one level, which is a good starting point for your own thinking. Discuss your ideas with your lab partner, sketch them on paper first, and only then move on to the computer. Your command-line interface should support these operations:
- Park a vehicle
- Remove a vehicle and print its fee
- Show the free spots on each level
